name: Frog Fights
description: Ostap Bender recently visited frog farm and was inspired to create his own frog game. Number of frogs are places on a cyclic gameboard, divided into m cells. Cells are numbered from 1 to m , but the board is cyclic, so cell number 1 goes right after the cell number m in the direction of movement. i -th frog during its turn can jump for a i cells. Frogs move in turns, game starts with a move by frog 1 . On its turn i -th frog moves a i cells forward, knocking out all the frogs on its way. If there is a frog in the last cell of the path of the i -th frog, that frog is also knocked out. After this the value a i is decreased by the number of frogs that were knocked out during this turn. If a i is zero or goes negative, then i -th frog doesn't make moves anymore. After frog number 1 finishes its turn, frog number 2 starts to move, then frog number 3 and so on. After the frog number n makes its move, frog 1 starts to move again, then frog 2 and so on this process goes forever. If some frog was already knocked out from the board, we consider that it skips all its moves. Help Ostap to identify, what frogs will stay on the board at the end of a game?
input_specification: First line of the input contains two integers n and m ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000, 1 ≤ m ≤ 10 9 , n ≤ m ) — number of frogs and gameboard size, respectively. Following n lines contains frogs descriptions — two integers p i and a i ( 1 ≤ p i , a i ≤ m ) — the number of cell occupied by i -th frog initially and initial jump length. All p i are guaranteed to be distinct.
output_specification: In the first line output number of frogs on the final gameboard. In the second line output their numbers in any order.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 625E — Frog Fights [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
